comm-systems-001.question: In wavelength-division multiplexing (WDM), which correctly describes how the transmission capacity of a single optical fiber is increased?
choices: One signal is split over several wavelengths sent at the same time, and the receiver adds them together to raise the received power and so the bit rate that can be sent above the noise
Separate signals are placed on laser beams of different frequencies, combined into one fiber, and separated by wavelength at the receiver
Light at a single wavelength is divided finely in time, and several signals are packed into it in turn, multiplexing them without adding wavelengths
comm-systems-001.explanation: WDM relies on the fact that light at different frequencies propagates through a linear medium without affecting each other, and places an independent signal on each wavelength. A multiplexer combines them into one fiber, and at the receiver a demultiplexer such as thin-film filters or an arrayed waveguide grating separates them by wavelength for separate detection, so the capacity is roughly the bit rate per wavelength times the number of wavelengths. Sending the same signal on several wavelengths only divides the power and does not raise capacity. Packing signals in time slots is time-division multiplexing (TDM), a different kind of multiplexing used within one wavelength. Real systems combine the two.

comm-systems-002.question: Near a wavelength of 1550 nm, WDM channels are placed at a frequency spacing of 50 GHz. Which is closest to this spacing expressed in wavelength? (c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s)
choices: About 0.4 nm
About 0.8 nm
About 0.04 nm
comm-systems-002.explanation: Frequency spacing converts to wavelength spacing as Δλ = λ²Δf/c. Δλ = (1550×10⁻⁹)² × 50×10⁹ / 3.0×10⁸ ≈ 4.0×10⁻¹⁰ m, or about 0.4 nm. About 0.8 nm is the value for a 100 GHz spacing; it is easy to confuse because 100 GHz corresponds to roughly 0.8 nm near 1550 nm. About 0.04 nm is an order-of-magnitude error. WDM channels are normally placed at equal frequency intervals, and since the wavelength spacing is proportional to λ², it becomes slightly narrower toward shorter wavelengths.

comm-systems-003.question: Why did the EDFA make WDM transmission with many wavelengths practical?
choices: It demultiplexes and detects each channel, reshapes the waveform electrically and retransmits it (regenerative repeating), so no noise accumulates at all along the link
It selects and boosts only one wavelength, so crosstalk and four-wave-mixing light from neighboring channels are removed
A single unit amplifies the many channels within its gain band of tens of nm in the 1.55 µm region at once, without converting them back to electrical signals
comm-systems-003.explanation: An EDFA amplifies light as light, through stimulated emission from population-inverted erbium ions. Its gain spans tens of nm centered on the C band (about 1530–1565 nm) in the 1.55 µm region, so one unit can amplify well over tens of channels at once, independent of the signal bit rate and modulation format. Demultiplexing, reshaping electrically and retransmitting is how regenerative repeaters worked before EDFAs; they needed a receiver and transmitter for every channel, which made scaling WDM difficult. An EDFA also amplifies spontaneous emission (ASE), so noise does accumulate at each repeater. It is not a device that picks out and amplifies just one wavelength.

comm-systems-004.question: In long-haul WDM transmission with many cascaded EDFAs, what is the main purpose of inserting a gain-flattening filter (GFF)?
choices: To remove only the pump wavelength (980 nm or 1480 nm) so that the EDFA pump light does not reach the receiver along with the signal and add noise
The EDFA gain varies with wavelength, and per-channel differences in power and OSNR add up over many stages, so the filter cancels them to equalize the channels
To remove unwanted frequency components between channels so that the spacing to neighboring channels can be narrowed and more channels can be packed into the same amplifier band
comm-systems-004.explanation: The EDFA gain spectrum is not flat: it has a sharp peak near 1530 nm and is gentler on the long-wavelength side. Even a small difference per stage adds up; for example, a 1 dB difference over 10 stages becomes 10 dB, so low-gain channels run short of OSNR while high-gain channels suffer more from nonlinearity. A filter whose loss spectrum is the inverse of the gain shape is therefore built into the amplifier to equalize the gain of all channels. Separating or combining pump and signal is the job of the wavelength-multiplexing coupler, not the purpose of a GFF. Channel spacing is set by the transmitter frequencies and the characteristics of the multiplexers and demultiplexers.

comm-systems-005.question: An optical link has a transmitter output of 0 dBm and a receiver sensitivity of −24 dBm. Connector losses total 1 dB, a system margin of 3 dB is reserved, and the fiber loss (including fusion splices) is 0.25 dB/km. Which is closest to the maximum transmission distance set by loss?
choices: About 92 km
About 96 km
About 80 km
comm-systems-005.explanation: The loss budget (power budget) is the difference between transmitter output and receiver sensitivity, 0 − (−24) = 24 dB. Subtracting the 1 dB of connectors and a 3 dB margin for component aging, temperature changes and repair splices leaves 24 − 1 − 3 = 20 dB for the fiber, so the distance is 20 / 0.25 = 80 km. About 92 km forgets to subtract the margin, and about 96 km ignores every loss other than the fiber. In real designs the budget also includes the extra received power needed to keep the same error rate in the presence of chromatic dispersion and other impairments (the power penalty), and the distance is chosen to satisfy both the loss and the dispersion conditions.

comm-systems-006.question: The accumulated dispersion of 80 km of single-mode fiber with a chromatic dispersion of 17 ps/(nm·km) is to be cancelled exactly with dispersion-compensating fiber (DCF) of −100 ps/(nm·km). Which is closest to the required DCF length?
choices: About 13.6 km
About 80 km
About 1.36 km
comm-systems-006.explanation: The accumulated dispersion of the link is 17 × 80 = 1360 ps/nm. With a DCF length L, −100 × L = −1360 ps/nm gives L = 13.6 km. About 80 km assumes the same length as the link is needed and ignores the ratio of the dispersion magnitudes. About 1.36 km is an order-of-magnitude error. DCF has higher loss than ordinary fiber (at 0.5 dB/km, for example, 13.6 km adds about 6.8 dB), and its small core makes nonlinearity more likely, so it was commonly placed between the stages of a two-stage EDFA. In transmission with coherent detection, dispersion is compensated by digital signal processing at the receiver, so configurations without DCF are also possible.

comm-systems-007.question: Keeping the same symbol rate, a link changes from binary intensity modulation (NRZ) to four-level intensity modulation (PAM4). Which correctly describes the change? (The range between minimum and maximum optical intensity is the same.)
choices: Four levels are used, so each symbol carries 4 bits and the bit rate becomes four times higher, with the required SNR unchanged
The bit rate doubles and the spectral width also doubles, so a wider-band receiver is needed, while the required SNR goes down
Each symbol carries 2 bits, so the bit rate doubles, but the level spacing drops to 1/3, so a higher SNR is needed for the same error rate
comm-systems-007.explanation: PAM4 uses four intensity levels and sends log₂4 = 2 bits per symbol, so at the same symbol rate the bit rate doubles. Fitting four levels into the same intensity range splits it into three gaps, each 1/3 of the NRZ spacing, so errors become more likely for the same noise. In terms of the electrical SNR of the received signal this is a penalty of 20 log₁₀3 ≈ 9.5 dB; when thermal noise dominates, the received optical power must be raised by about 4.8 dB (10 log₁₀3). The number of bits doubles; it does not quadruple. The spectral width is set mainly by the symbol rate, so at the same symbol rate it does not grow, and the advantage of PAM4 is that the bit rate can be raised while keeping bandwidth-limited components.

comm-systems-008.question: When dispersion-shifted fiber with nearly zero chromatic dispersion near 1550 nm is used for WDM transmission, problems between channels are likely. What is the main cause?
choices: Without dispersion the effect of birefringence is not cancelled, so polarization-mode dispersion grows and the delay of each channel varies, causing intersymbol interference
Without dispersion the channels stay in phase as they propagate, so four-wave mixing occurs efficiently and the generated light falls on other channels as crosstalk
Without dispersion the pulses do not spread and keep a high peak power, so they exceed the stimulated Brillouin scattering threshold and all channels are reflected back toward the input
comm-systems-008.explanation: Four-wave mixing (FWM) is the process by which third-order nonlinearity generates light at f_i + f_j − f_k from light at frequencies f_i, f_j and f_k. Its efficiency is set by phase matching between the channels: large chromatic dispersion quickly destroys the phase relationship and weakens it, but with nearly zero dispersion it stays well matched and FWM is strong. With equally spaced channels, the generated light lands exactly on other channel frequencies and becomes crosstalk that cannot be removed. This is why non-zero dispersion-shifted fiber, which leaves a small dispersion at 1550 nm, is used. Polarization-mode dispersion is set by fiber birefringence, a property separate from the size of chromatic dispersion. Stimulated Brillouin scattering is backscattering caused by strong narrow-linewidth light and is not determined by whether dispersion is present.

comm-systems-009.question: For a link of N identical spans, the OSNR measured in a 0.1 nm noise bandwidth can be estimated as OSNR[dB] ≈ 58 + P_ch − L_span − NF − 10 log₁₀N (P_ch is the input power per channel [dBm], L_span the span loss [dB], NF the EDFA noise figure [dB]). With P_ch = 0 dBm, L_span = 22 dB, NF = 5 dB and N = 10, which is closest to the OSNR?
choices: About 21 dB
About 31 dB
About 11 dB
comm-systems-009.explanation: Substituting gives 58 + 0 − 22 − 5 − 10 log₁₀10 = 58 − 22 − 5 − 10 = 21 dB. The constant 58 comes from the product of the photon energy at 1550 nm, hν ≈ 1.28×10⁻¹⁹ J, and the reference bandwidth of 12.5 GHz (0.1 nm), which is about −58 dBm. Each EDFA adds the same amount of ASE noise, so the noise power is proportional to the number of spans and the OSNR falls by 10 log₁₀N. About 31 dB forgets the degradation from the number of spans, and about 11 dB subtracts it twice as 20 log₁₀N. The required OSNR is set by the modulation format and error correction; if it is not met, raise the input power or shorten the spans.

comm-systems-010.question: A 1200 km link with a loss of 0.2 dB/km is built either with EDFAs every 60 km (20 spans) or every 120 km (10 spans). Using the estimate OSNR[dB] ≈ 58 + P_ch − L_span − NF − 10 log₁₀N, with the same input power and NF, which correctly describes the difference in OSNR?
choices: The 120 km spacing is about 3 dB higher
The 60 km spacing is about 9 dB higher
Both have the same total loss of 240 dB, so they are equal
comm-systems-010.explanation: A 60 km span has 12 dB of loss with 20 stages, and a 120 km span has 24 dB with 10 stages. The OSNR difference is (−12 − 10 log₁₀20) − (−24 − 10 log₁₀10) = (−12 − 13.0) − (−34) ≈ 9 dB, so the 60 km spacing is about 9 dB higher. Span loss counts directly in dB while the number of stages counts only as 10 log₁₀N, so shorter spans win. Saying the 120 km spacing is better looks only at the halved number of amplifiers acting as noise sources, a gain of about 3 dB, and overlooks that each amplifier must make up 12 dB (about 16 times) more loss. Even with the same total loss, noise is added at each amplifier in proportion to its gain, so the two are not equal.

comm-systems-011.question: Which is closest to the line bit rate (including error-correction overhead) when dual-polarization 16QAM (DP-16QAM) is sent at a symbol rate of 32 GBd?
choices: About 256 Gb/s
About 128 Gb/s
About 1024 Gb/s
comm-systems-011.explanation: 16QAM uses 16 constellation points formed by combinations of amplitude and phase, so each symbol carries log₂16 = 4 bits. Polarization multiplexing, which places separate signals on two orthogonal polarizations, doubles this again: 4 × 2 × 32 GBd = 256 Gb/s. About 128 Gb/s forgets the factor of 2 from polarization multiplexing, and about 1024 Gb/s mistakenly multiplies by the 16 points as if they were bits. The net data rate actually carried is this value minus the error-correction overhead, so this example corresponds to 200 Gb/s-class transmission.

comm-systems-012.question: At the same symbol rate and the same average optical power, changing from QPSK to 16QAM raises the OSNR needed for the same error rate. What is the main reason?
choices: 16QAM has four times the symbol rate of QPSK, so the receiver bandwidth becomes four times wider and the noise power grows in proportion to the bandwidth
16QAM uses only 16 phases and not amplitude, so adjacent phases differ by only 22.5 degrees and it is more sensitive to noise
With more constellation points at the same average power, neighboring points are closer, so the same noise more easily makes one be mistaken for another
comm-systems-012.explanation: In the complex plane, QPSK has 4 points and 16QAM has 16 points on a 4×4 grid. At equal average power, the squared distance between neighboring points is 1/5 that of QPSK (10 log₁₀5 ≈ 7 dB), so under ideal conditions with only white Gaussian noise the SNR needed for the same error rate is about 7 dB higher (about 6.7 dB near an error rate of 10⁻³). The bits carried per symbol rise from 2 for QPSK to 4, but in exchange the reach becomes shorter. In this question the symbol rate is the same, so neither the signal bandwidth nor the noise bandwidth changes. 16QAM uses both amplitude and phase; it is PSK formats such as QPSK that use phase only.

comm-systems-013.question: Which correctly pairs the basic configuration of a digital coherent receiver with the information it obtains?
choices: No local oscillator is used; the phase of the signal and its two polarization components are read directly from the intensity detected by the square-law photodetector
The signal is mixed with a local oscillator in a 90° hybrid and detected with balanced photodetectors, giving the in-phase (I) and quadrature (Q) field components for each polarization
The local oscillator must be locked optically to the phase of the signal (optical phase locking), and digital signal processing cannot handle phase, so only intensity is obtained
comm-systems-013.explanation: A photodetector output is proportional to the optical intensity |E|², so on its own it reveals nothing about phase. When a local oscillator (LO) at a nearby frequency is superimposed on the signal, the interference term carries the signal amplitude and phase. A 90° hybrid produces two sets of interference with the LO phase shifted by 0 and π/2, and balanced photodetectors cancel the LO's own intensity, giving I and Q; doing this for two polarizations gives 4 outputs. Optical phase locking was once needed, but in digital receivers the frequency offset and phase fluctuations are estimated and removed by signal processing after A/D conversion, so the phase information can be demodulated without fixing the phase optically.

comm-systems-014.question: Why can the digital signal processing of a coherent receiver compensate chromatic dispersion accumulated over thousands of km?
choices: Chromatic dispersion is a linear change that only adds a phase to each frequency component, so once the field amplitude and phase are known, a filter applying the opposite phase restores it

Chromatic dispersion is a nonlinear change proportional to the optical intensity, so the waveform before dispersion can be uniquely calculated back from the received intensity waveform and optical power
Square-law detection by the photodetector erases phase information, so the effect of dispersion, which appears as a phase shift, disappears along with it and needs no compensation
comm-systems-014.explanation: The change caused by chromatic dispersion only multiplies the field spectrum by a phase exp(jβ₂Lω²/2) that is proportional to the square of the angular frequency, leaving the amplitude unchanged. This is a linear all-pass filter, and multiplying by the opposite phase restores the original. A coherent receiver obtains the field (I and Q of two polarizations) as digital values, so a filter with the inverse characteristic matched to the distance compensates it, and adaptive filters also separate polarization rotation and polarization-mode dispersion. Direct detection, which measures only intensity, loses the phase, and the field before dispersion cannot be recovered uniquely from the intensity waveform. It is nonlinear effects such as self-phase modulation, not dispersion, that depend on intensity. Square-law detection erases the phase, while the waveform distorted by dispersion remains.

comm-systems-015.question: In long-haul WDM transmission, as the input power per channel is raised, the effective SNR at the receiver reaches a maximum and then falls. Which correctly explains why?
choices: Raising the input power degrades the EDFA noise figure, so ASE noise grows as the cube of the power and the SNR falls beyond a certain input power
Raising the input power makes the fiber loss coefficient (dB/km) larger, so the received power levels off and the SNR against ASE noise starts to fall beyond a certain input power
The SNR against ASE noise improves in proportion to input power, but Kerr-effect nonlinear noise grows roughly as the cube of the power, so an optimum power balances the two
comm-systems-015.explanation: Amplifier ASE noise is nearly constant regardless of signal power, so raising the input power P improves the SNR against ASE in proportion to P. Meanwhile self-phase modulation, cross-phase modulation and four-wave mixing caused by the fiber Kerr effect behave like noise that disturbs the signal, with a magnitude roughly proportional to P³. The effective SNR takes the form P/(P_ASE + ηP³), so it peaks at the power where P_ASE = 2ηP³, and above that the nonlinear degradation wins. The EDFA noise figure is set mainly by the degree of population inversion and does not degrade as the cube of the input power. At these power levels the fiber loss coefficient is constant and does not depend on power.

comm-systems-016.question: In a 1550 nm intensity-modulation/direct-detection link without dispersion compensation, which is a correct advantage of using an external Mach-Zehnder modulator rather than directly modulating the semiconductor laser current?
choices: With direct modulation, the current changes the carrier density and refractive index, so the optical frequency fluctuates (chirp) and the spectrum broadens; the external modulator therefore suffers less degradation from chromatic dispersion
With direct modulation the laser output cannot keep up with the modulation speed, so an external modulator raises the receiver sensitivity and also reduces the transmission loss of the fiber itself
The external modulator changes the optical frequency strongly with the signal to broaden the spectrum, which suppresses four-wave mixing and eliminates the effect of chromatic dispersion
comm-systems-016.explanation: Changing the injection current of a semiconductor laser changes not only the optical power but also the carrier density in the active layer, which changes the refractive index and makes the lasing frequency fluctuate (chirp). Light with a broadened spectrum, after passing through fiber with large dispersion at 1550 nm, has its frequency components arrive at different times, so the pulse shape degrades quickly. A Mach-Zehnder modulator driven push-pull shifts the phases of its two arms in opposite directions and changes only the intensity, nearly eliminating chirp. Transmission loss is a property of the fiber and does not depend on the modulation method. An external modulator is not a device for broadening the spectrum, and a broader spectrum makes dispersion worse, not better.

comm-systems-017.question: In an intensity-modulation/direct-detection link without dispersion compensation, suppose the tolerable accumulated chromatic dispersion is inversely proportional to the square of the bit rate B. If 1000 ps/nm is tolerable at 10 Gb/s, which value is closest to the maximum transmission distance at 40 Gb/s with the same modulation format, over fiber with a dispersion of 17 ps/(nm·km)?
choices: About 15 km
About 59 km
About 3.7 km
comm-systems-017.explanation: The tolerable accumulated dispersion falls by (10/40)² = 1/16 to 1000/16 = 62.5 ps/nm. Dividing by 17 ps/(nm·km) gives about 3.7 km. At 10 Gb/s it was 1000/17 ≈ 59 km. Quadrupling the bit rate shortens the bit period to 1/4 and at the same time broadens the signal spectrum fourfold, so the dispersion-induced time spread also grows fourfold; the tolerance therefore drops to 1/16. About 15 km assumes inverse proportionality to B, reducing by 1/4, and about 59 km ignores the effect of the bit rate. For this reason high-speed links use the low-dispersion 1310 nm band, dispersion compensation, or the digital signal processing of coherent receivers.

comm-systems-018.question: For a received signal whose Q factor (the difference between the means of the two levels divided by the sum of the two noise standard deviations) is 6, which value is closest to the bit error rate assuming Gaussian noise, BER = (1/2)erfc(Q/√2)?
choices: About 1×10⁻¹⁷
About 1×10⁻⁹
About 1×10⁻⁵
comm-systems-018.explanation: Q/√2 = 6/1.414 ≈ 4.24, and erfc(4.24) ≈ 2.0×10⁻⁹, so BER ≈ 1.0×10⁻⁹. For large Q, BER ≈ exp(−Q²/2)/(Q√(2π)), and exp(−18)/(6 × 2.51) ≈ 1.0×10⁻⁹ confirms it. About 1×10⁻¹⁷ forgets to divide by √2 and uses erfc(6); about 1×10⁻⁵ divides by 2 instead of √2. The BER changes very steeply with Q, reaching about 1×10⁻¹² at Q = 7, so Q is expressed in dB (20 log₁₀Q) to manage margins. In practice, forward error correction can deliver error-free output even when the pre-correction BER is around 10⁻³.

comm-systems-019.question: When a polarization-multiplexed signal is transmitted, its polarization state changes randomly with time in the fiber. Why can a digital coherent receiver separate the two polarization tributaries without optically aligning the polarization at the receiver?
choices: Because it measures the fields in both polarizations, it can keep estimating the inverse of the 2×2 matrix describing the fiber's polarization rotation with an adaptive digital filter and apply it

Although polarization rotates in the fiber, a polarization-maintaining property keeps the directions at transmitter and receiver always identical, so the receiver only needs a polarizer at a fixed orientation
The two polarization tributaries are carried on slightly different frequencies, so the receiver separates them with frequency filters, and polarization changes in the fiber do not affect the signals
comm-systems-019.explanation: Without loss or polarization-dependent loss, the fiber's effect on polarization is a 2×2 unitary Jones matrix. A coherent receiver mixes the received light with a local oscillator and obtains I and Q for each of two orthogonal polarizations, that is, both components of the field. A 2×2 butterfly adaptive filter can therefore estimate the inverse of this matrix and, by continually updating its coefficients from the received signal, track the time-varying polarization rotation and separate the two signals. The same filter also compensates polarization mode dispersion. Polarization changes with temperature and vibration, so a polarizer at a fixed orientation cannot separate the signals. Polarization multiplexing places different signals on two orthogonal polarizations at the same frequency.

comm-systems-020.question: A signal at a symbol rate of 32 GBd is shaped to a raised-cosine spectrum with roll-off factor β so that WDM channels can be packed closely (Nyquist WDM). Which statement about making β smaller is correct?
choices: The signal bandwidth is fixed at twice the symbol rate, 64 GHz, independent of β, so the channel spacing cannot be reduced and only intersymbol interference increases
As β approaches 0 the intersymbol interference grows and the Nyquist criterion is violated, so intersymbol interference vanishes only when β = 1
The occupied bandwidth Rs(1 + β) approaches 32 GHz, so channels can be placed at narrower spacing without overlapping, but the shaping filters become longer and steeper
comm-systems-020.explanation: A raised-cosine spectrum satisfies the Nyquist criterion for every β, giving zero intersymbol interference at the sampling instants. The optical signal occupies a bandwidth of Rs(1 + β): at 32 GBd, about 35 GHz for β = 0.1 and 64 GHz for β = 1. Making β smaller brings the bandwidth close to the symbol rate, so channels do not overlap even at a narrow spacing such as 37.5 GHz. In exchange, the time-domain waveform has longer tails, the digital filters at transmitter and receiver need more taps, and the system becomes more sensitive to timing errors. A bandwidth of 2Rs confuses it with the main-lobe width of the spectrum of unshaped rectangular pulses. Intersymbol interference is not absent only at β = 1.

comm-systems-021.question: An optical signal sent as dual-polarization 16QAM at 64 GBd has a line rate of 512 Gb/s. If the overhead for forward error correction and similar functions is 28% of the information bit rate (information bit rate × 1.28 = line rate), which value is closest to the net information bit rate?
choices: About 369 Gb/s
About 400 Gb/s
About 655 Gb/s
comm-systems-021.explanation: The overhead is 28% of the information rate, so the information rate is 512/1.28 = 400 Gb/s. About 369 Gb/s is 512 × (1 − 0.28), subtracting 28% of the line rate, which misreads the definition of overhead. About 655 Gb/s multiplies by 1.28 by mistake. The soft-decision FEC used in coherent transmission can turn a pre-FEC bit error ratio of about 10⁻³ to 10⁻² into nearly error-free output, greatly lowering the required OSNR. In exchange, about 20% of redundant bits are sent, so the line rate is higher than the net rate.

comm-systems-022.question: In a passive optical network (PON), one fiber is split into 32 by an optical splitter to serve individual homes. For an ideal lossless 1:32 splitter, which value is closest to the splitting loss at each output?
choices: About 32 dB
About 30 dB
About 15 dB
comm-systems-022.explanation: An ideal splitter divides the power into 32 equal parts, so each output receives 1/32 and the loss is 10 log₁₀32 ≈ 15 dB. Real splitters add an excess loss of about 1 to 2 dB. About 30 dB uses 20 log₁₀, applying the formula for voltage or amplitude ratios to a power ratio. About 32 dB simply takes the split count as dB. In a PON, the downstream signal from the central office reaches every home identically, and each home's equipment picks out its own part. Upstream, homes send in turn in assigned time slots, so the receiver at the office must handle bursts of differing strength.

comm-systems-023.question: Wavelength-selective switches in ROADMs use a flexible grid that assigns channel bandwidth in widths of 12.5 GHz units instead of a fixed 50 GHz grid. Which is the main reason?
choices: Each signal can be given the width it needs (for example 75 GHz), so high-symbol-rate signals that do not fit in 50 GHz can pass and the spectrum is used without waste
A 12.5 GHz grid lets signals of any symbol rate be packed four times as densely, so the capacity simply quadruples
A finer grid splits the EDFA gain band into flat 12.5 GHz pieces, so gain-flattening filters are no longer needed even over many amplified spans
comm-systems-023.explanation: A signal occupies roughly its symbol rate plus a roll-off margin. A 64 GBd signal, for example, occupies about 70 GHz including roll-off and does not fit in a 50 GHz slot, and even a 32 GBd signal leaves unused space at the slot edges. A flexible grid sets the center and width of each wavelength-selective-switch passband in fine steps and assigns each signal only the width it needs, so the fiber spectrum is packed tightly. More channels fit only when the signals are narrower than the slots; capacity does not quadruple for every signal. The grid spacing is about how the switch allocates bandwidth and has nothing to do with the shape of the EDFA gain.

comm-systems-024.question: In digital coherent reception, which correctly describes how the linewidth (phase noise) of the transmitter laser and the local-oscillator laser affects reception?
choices: Phase noise is a linear change that leaves the amplitude untouched, so a fixed inverse filter, as for chromatic dispersion, removes it completely, and laser linewidth does not matter
The lower the symbol rate and the longer each symbol, the more the phase fluctuation averages out within it, so broader-linewidth lasers become easier to use
DSP carrier-phase estimation tracks the phase fluctuation, but higher-order QAM has narrower phase spacing between points, so the linewidth–symbol-time product must be kept small
comm-systems-024.explanation: The phases of both lasers wander randomly according to their linewidths. In a coherent receiver the phase difference to the local oscillator changes with time, so DSP estimates the carrier phase and undoes the rotation of the constellation. The faster the phase wanders, the harder the estimate is to keep up, and in 16QAM or 64QAM, with narrow phase spacing between points, even a small residual error causes misdecisions. The impact is set by the product of linewidth and symbol time, so lowering the symbol rate to lengthen each symbol actually lets more phase change accumulate. Phase noise changes randomly with time, so a fixed filter cannot remove it.

comm-systems-025.question: In an intensity-modulation direct-detection transmitter, if the extinction ratio (ratio of the optical powers of the 1 and 0 levels) is not large enough, receiver sensitivity worsens even when the average optical power is kept the same. Which is the correct reason?
choices: Light in the 0 level is constant like detector dark current, so subtracting it at the receiver removes its effect, and only the transmitter's power consumption suffers
Because light remains in the 0 level, the difference between the 1 and 0 powers shrinks relative to the average, so a higher average power is needed for the same error rate
Light in the 0 level is moved into the time of the 1 levels by self-phase modulation and other nonlinear effects in the fiber, causing intersymbol interference with neighboring bits
comm-systems-025.explanation: What lets the receiver tell 1 from 0 is the difference between the two levels. With average power P, the difference is 2P(r − 1)/(r + 1), where r is the extinction ratio, smaller than the 2P obtained with an infinite extinction ratio. Keeping the same difference requires (r + 1)/(r − 1) times the average power, so an extinction ratio of 10 dB (r = 10) costs 10 log₁₀(11/9) ≈ 0.9 dB. Subtracting a constant 0 level does not widen the eye, and light in the 0 level also adds shot noise and beat noise with optical amplifier noise. At normal powers, nonlinear effects do not move 0-level light into other time slots.

comm-systems-026.question: For a channel with additive white Gaussian noise, the upper limit on the information that can be sent without error per unit bandwidth (the Shannon limit) is C/B = log₂(1 + SNR). When the SNR is 20 dB, which value is closest to this limit? (Consider a single polarization.)
choices: About 6.7 b/(s·Hz)
About 4.4 b/(s·Hz)
About 2.0 b/(s·Hz)
comm-systems-026.explanation: 20 dB is a ratio of 10^(20/10) = 100, so C/B = log₂(1 + 100) = log₂101 ≈ 6.66, about 6.7 b/(s·Hz). About 4.4 b/(s·Hz) wrongly uses the dB value 20 as the ratio and computes log₂21, and about 2.0 b/(s·Hz) uses base 10 instead of base 2, log₁₀101. With polarization multiplexing, twice this can be sent using both polarizations. Real combinations of modulation format and error correction carry less than the Shannon limit at the same SNR, and higher-order modulation with strong error correction is used to approach it. In optical fiber, raising the power increases nonlinear noise, so there is also a limit to increasing capacity by raising the SNR.

comm-systems-027.question: A receiver at 1550 nm operating at 10 Gb/s has a sensitivity of −30 dBm (average optical power). Which value is closest to the average number of photons received per bit? (h = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ J·s, c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s)
choices: About 7.8×10¹²
About 780
About 0.78
comm-systems-027.explanation: −30 dBm is 10^(−30/10) mW = 1.0 µW. One photon carries hc/λ ≈ 1.28×10⁻¹⁹ J, so 1.0×10⁻⁶/1.28×10⁻¹⁹ ≈ 7.8×10¹² photons arrive per second, and dividing by 10¹⁰ bits per second gives about 780 photons per bit. About 7.8×10¹² is the number per second, not divided by the bit rate. About 0.78 mistakes −30 dBm for 1 nW. In a direct-detection receiver, thermal noise in the receiver circuit adds to the shot noise, so far more photons are needed than the shot-noise limit (an average of about 10 photons per bit for a bit error rate of 10⁻⁹).

comm-systems-028.question: Coarse wavelength division multiplexing (CWDM), used in data centers and short-reach optical links, uses a wide channel spacing of about 20 nm. Which combination of main advantage and limitation is correct?
choices: The wide spacing allows more channels than dense WDM, and a single EDFA amplifies them all together, so it is used for long-haul, high-capacity transmission
The wide spacing prevents four-wave mixing and removes the effects of fiber loss and dispersion, so it works over any distance with no repeaters
Laser wavelength drift with temperature does not reach the next channel, so uncooled lasers and cheap multiplexers can be used, but there are few channels
comm-systems-028.explanation: The wavelength of a DFB laser shifts by about 0.1 nm/K, so it moves by several nanometers over 0–70 °C. Dense WDM (0.4 nm or 0.8 nm spacing) requires cooling to hold the temperature constant, but with 20 nm spacing the drift does not reach the next channel, so cheap lasers without coolers and inexpensive wide-band filters can be used. On the other hand, even spanning roughly 1270–1610 nm gives only a dozen or so channels, and only one or two fall within the EDFA gain band (about 35 nm), so CWDM is not suited to amplified long-haul transmission. Loss and dispersion do not disappear: loss is higher at the short-wavelength end and dispersion at the long-wavelength end, so reach is limited to a few to a few tens of kilometers.

comm-systems-029.question: In a gain-saturated EDFA carrying many WDM channels, a fault suddenly removes many of the channels. Which combination of what happens to the surviving channels without countermeasures and the countermeasure is correct?
choices: Total output stays roughly constant, so the surviving channels' powers jump and the effect builds up over cascaded amplifiers; fast pump control keeps the gain constant
EDFA gain is always constant regardless of the number of channels, so the surviving channels' powers do not change at all and no special measures are needed at the receiver
EDFA gain drops in proportion to the number of channels, so the surviving channels' powers fall and the receiver sensitivity becomes insufficient, so the receiver gain is raised
comm-systems-029.explanation: In a saturated EDFA, the channels share a total output power set by the pump. When many channels disappear, the input drops, the saturation eases and the gain rises, so the surviving channels leave with a bigger share of power. This change follows the erbium response within tens of microseconds to milliseconds, and when it accumulates over many amplifiers it causes errors through nonlinear impairments and overloading of receivers. Automatic gain control is therefore used: input and output powers are monitored and the pump current is adjusted quickly to keep the gain constant as the channel count changes. Saying the gain is independent of channel count ignores saturation, and saying it falls has the direction reversed.

comm-systems-030.question: When many WDM channels are amplified together in a semiconductor optical amplifier (SOA), signals leak between channels (crosstalk), but this is not a problem in an EDFA. Which is the main reason for the difference?
choices: An SOA has a narrow gain band, so channels at the band edges lack gain, and the signals of high-gain channels move into low-gain channels
SOA gain responds in a nanosecond or less and follows the bit-by-bit intensity, whereas EDFA gain responds on a millisecond scale and does not follow the bits
An EDFA amplifies the two polarizations separately, which keeps the channels apart, whereas an SOA amplifies all channels in the same polarization, so they mix
comm-systems-030.explanation: In an SOA the carrier lifetime is about 100 ps to 1 ns, so the gain changes quickly with the ones and zeros of one channel, and that change is imprinted on the other channels sharing the gain (cross-gain modulation). In an EDFA the upper-level lifetime of erbium is long, about 10 ms, so the gain cannot follow Gb/s signals and is set by the average input power, and no bit-by-bit crosstalk arises. The SOA gain band is broad, tens of nanometers, so a narrow band is not the cause, and an EDFA does not amplify each polarization separately. The fast response of an SOA is, conversely, exploited for optical signal processing such as wavelength conversion.

comm-systems-031.question: WDM channels are placed at 50 GHz spacing across a 4.0 THz band, and each channel carries a polarization-multiplexed signal at 200 Gb/s (the net value for both polarizations together). Which combination correctly gives the total capacity of one fiber and the spectral efficiency?
choices: About 16 Tb/s; 4 b/(s·Hz)
About 32 Tb/s; 8 b/(s·Hz)
About 8 Tb/s; 2 b/(s·Hz)
comm-systems-031.explanation: The number of channels is 4.0 THz/50 GHz = 80, so the total capacity is 80 × 200 Gb/s = 16 Tb/s. The spectral efficiency is 200 Gb/s per 50 GHz channel, 200/50 = 4 b/(s·Hz), the same as 16 Tb/s ÷ 4.0 THz. About 32 Tb/s doubles again for polarization multiplexing although the 200 Gb/s already covers both polarizations. About 8 Tb/s halves the channel count by assuming each channel occupies 50 GHz on each side of its center, 100 GHz in total. Capacity can be raised further by narrowing the spacing, using higher-order modulation, or adding the L band to the C band.

comm-systems-032.question: With coherent reception, a signal whose OSNR measured in a 0.1 nm (12.5 GHz) noise bandwidth is 20 dB is received at a symbol rate of 32 GBd. Estimating the SNR in the signal bandwidth as SNR ≈ OSNR × (12.5 GHz/symbol rate), which value is closest to the SNR?
choices: About 24 dB
About 16 dB
About 20 dB
comm-systems-032.explanation: 12.5/32 ≈ 0.39 is 10 log₁₀0.39 ≈ −4.1 dB, so SNR ≈ 20 − 4.1 ≈ 15.9 dB, about 16 dB. OSNR is measured with the noise in a fixed 0.1 nm bandwidth; when the signal occupies a wider band of about 32 GHz, more noise falls within the receiver bandwidth, and the SNR is correspondingly lower than the OSNR. About 24 dB inverts the ratio and adds 4.1 dB. About 20 dB ignores the bandwidth difference. Doubling the symbol rate lowers the SNR by about 3 dB at the same OSNR, so higher-symbol-rate signals need a higher OSNR.

comm-systems-033.question: When many WDM channels spanning the C and L bands are launched with high total power, the channel powers after transmission become tilted with wavelength (power tilt). Which correctly gives the cause and the direction of this effect?
choices: Four-wave mixing transfers power from the long-wavelength channels to the short-wavelength ones, so the short-wavelength side becomes stronger
Fiber loss increases with wavelength, so after transmission the long-wavelength side is weaker and the short-wavelength side stronger
Stimulated Raman scattering moves power from short- to long-wavelength channels, so the long-wavelength side becomes stronger
comm-systems-033.explanation: Stimulated Raman scattering in silica transfers energy from higher-frequency light to a broad range of lower frequencies centered about 13 THz below. When WDM channels span several terahertz or more with high total power, the short-wavelength (higher-frequency) channels act as pumps that amplify the long-wavelength ones, so after transmission the long-wavelength side is stronger and the short-wavelength side weaker. The tilt grows with total power and bandwidth, so it is corrected by pre-tilting the launch powers or by amplifiers with adjustable gain tilt. Loss near 1550 nm is nearly flat and does not increase with wavelength there. Four-wave mixing creates light at new frequencies and does not cause such a one-way power transfer.

comm-systems-034.question: Probabilistic shaping keeps a constellation such as 64QAM unchanged but uses the low-energy points near the center more often and the outer points less often. Which describes its effect correctly?
choices: At the same average power the points can be spaced farther apart, approaching the Shannon limit, and the information per symbol can be tuned finely
Using the outer points less lowers the signal peaks and nonlinear noise, but the information per symbol stays at 6 bits, the same as 64QAM
Because the frequently used points are known in advance, the receiver no longer needs phase estimation, removing the linewidth requirement on the local-oscillator laser
comm-systems-034.explanation: On an additive white Gaussian noise channel, the input that maximizes capacity is a Gaussian-distributed signal. Ordinary QAM with equally likely points departs from this and leaves a gap to the Shannon limit. Probabilistic shaping uses the low-energy inner points more often to approach a Gaussian distribution; at the same average power the whole constellation can then be scaled up (points spaced farther apart), lowering the SNR needed for the same error rate. Changing the probability distribution sets the information per symbol to any value below 6 bits, so capacity can be matched finely to the transmission distance. Skewing the probabilities makes the entropy less than 6 bits, so the claim that it stays at 6 bits is wrong. Nor does shaping remove the need for phase estimation.

comm-systems-035.question: In an intensity-modulation direct-detection (IM-DD) link without dispersion compensation, double-sideband modulation, which creates sidebands on both sides of the optical carrier, makes the received electrical signal fade deeply at particular frequencies because of fiber chromatic dispersion. Which explains this correctly?
choices: Dispersion rotates the sideband polarization, and the electrical signal shrinks at frequencies where it reaches the polarization the photodetector senses least
Dispersion broadens the pulses and causes intersymbol interference, so the strength falls uniformly at higher frequencies and no fading at particular frequencies occurs
Dispersion shifts the phases of the two carrier beat notes from the upper and lower sidebands in opposite directions, and the electrical signal fades where they cancel
comm-systems-035.explanation: Double-sideband modulation creates sidebands above and below the carrier, separated from it by the modulation frequency f, and in the photodetector each beats with the carrier to give an electrical signal at f. Chromatic dispersion imposes a phase proportional to the square of the frequency offset from the carrier, so both sidebands are phase-shifted in the same direction, while their beat notes with the carrier shift in opposite directions, and the phase difference between the two beat notes grows in proportion to the accumulated dispersion and to f². At frequencies where the difference reaches π the beat notes cancel and the electrical signal fades deeply; the longer the link, the lower the first fading frequency. Single-sideband modulation or coherent reception avoids this fading. Dispersion does not rotate polarization, and a merely uniform roll-off misses the fading notches.
